Would Rather, Would Sooner, Would Have Preferred
You use Would rather/Would sooner + Simple Past or Would have preferred to+ infinitive to talk about preferences in the present or the future.

You use Would rather/Would sooner+ Simple Past to talk about a preference or strong advice in the present or the future. In this case, you can use it to talk about when you want someone else to do something
Examples: I'd rather you focused on customer service.
Vanessa would sooner I stayed in the kitchen.

You also use would have preferred to + infinitive to express preference or advice.
Example: I would have preferred to receive higher ratings.

You can use the expression It's high time + Past Simple to express a preference about the past or the present.
Example: It's high time we changed our menu.
I would have preferred to know how to separate emotions from the work at hand when dealing with employees.
I would rather have focused on tasks and results rather than my employee's negative personality traits.
Managers, myself included would sooner turn away from their least favorite employees than interact with them.
It's high time I confronted problems head-on.

You use modals like should or ought to to give advice.
You use would with an -if clause to give advice and suggestions about a hypothetical situation.
The most common modals for giving advice are: should, ought to and would.
You can think of modals as “helping verbs”. They add meaning to the main verb of a sentence. In this case, these modals add the meaning of advice.

Should is the most common modal used to give advice.
Ought to is used for giving strong advice.
Would can be used with an -if clause to give a personal advice or suggestion as a hypothetical situation, like If I were you, I would ...

images.text: Managing someone with whom you have a personality clash can cause major tension. I would have preferred to know how to separate emotions from the work at hand when dealing with employees. I would rather have focused on tasks and results rather than my employee's negative personality traits. Managers shouldn't allow their personal feelings to interfere, and ought to treat everyone the same way. But in too many cases, managers, myself included, would sooner turn away from their least favorite employees than interact with them.
When confronted with employees who don't do what's asked, managers ought to devise a strategy for making the best of a potentially explosive situation.
It's high time I confronted problems head-on. Clearing the air and calmly acknowledging any ill will can help everyone focus on getting the job done.
Seek confirmation. When giving instructions, you shouldn't assume you're making yourself clear. If I were you, I would make sure the employee knows what's expected of them.

Rehearse. Making simple requests is painless. But when you must explain something more complicated, don't wing it. You shouldn't waste time backtracking or jumbling words. I would rather use the fewest words possible to describe the goal.

Speak and write. To ensure the employee understands you, you ought to assign tasks both orally and in print. It's time I got in the habit of talking with that person and telling them what I need. You ought to let the employee ask questions and offer suggestions. Then, follow up soon after the discussion with an e-mail or memo that summarizes what's expected.

When managing someone with an attitude problem, you wouldn't let the person's personality interfere with the job at hand. Focus on describing the work that you need done. The employee would sooner I avoided making any quips about their track record on complying with my past requests.
